sourceHtml:
Wed, Nov 4, 2026, 20:30 CET

Incident post mortem

Summary

On 2 November 2026, an attacker gained unauthorized access to GitBook’s systems.

Using a flaw in GitBook’s SSO login flow, they were able to create login sessions acting as GitBook staff. This allowed them to query the authentication information of a misconfigured GitHub App installed as an integration in our organization, gaining access to our internal code repositories and, eventually, a Cloudflare API key.

Using this key, they gained access to production secrets which granted full infrastructure access through a service account.

Within hours, we disabled every affected internal infrastructure service account. That stopped the attack, and it also took the GitBook app offline. We then rotated every secret and API key in our infrastructure, and every customer secret managed by GitBook. GitBook was fully back online at 11:56 UTC on 3 November, after about 16 hours of downtime.

Everything we’ve seen points to an attack aimed at one GitBook customer rather than at GitBook as a whole. We have found no evidence that any other customer’s content was modified. 

While they had access, the attacker could reach customer data stored in GitBook. So we’ve treated all customer data as exposed, not only the targeted customer. 

How we contained the incident and restored service

Taking GitBook offline was a deliberate decision. Once the attacker was in our cloud infrastructure, keeping the platform running meant they could keep looking for access while we worked. We chose a longer outage over that risk.

While offline, we rotated every secret in our production infrastructure and every GitBook-managed customer secret, invalidated all API tokens issued before our final cutoff, recycled all nodes in staging and production, and reversed everything the compromised service account had done. We also disabled our back office while we strengthened its safeguards.

This incident is on us. We’re sorry, both for the disruption and for not communicating with you sooner.

The next section sets out exactly what was accessible, what we found, and what we’ve done about it.

What this means for your data

The attacker had access to our production environment for about 2:45 hours on the evening of 2 November, and about 40 minutes early on 3 November. 

During that time, the following customer data was accessible to them:

  • GitBook API tokens

  • Integration tokens and secrets

  • Session signing secrets 

  • Questions asked to GitBook Assistant by your site visitors

  • Documentation sites using authenticated access

  • GitHub 

    • Further info: the attacker could act as the GitBook app, but only in the repositories each customer had given the app access to. We cannot determine whether they took any action in customer repositories. We have suggested remedial steps below.

  • GitLab

    • Further info: the attacker could act on GitBook’s behalf in connected GitLab projects temporarily, but only in the repositories each customer had granted access to. We cannot determine whether they took any action in customer repositories. We have suggested remedial steps below.

  • Your content, such as docs, spaces and change requests

    • Further info: we have found no evidence that any other customer’s content was modified

Billing information, passwords or IP addresses have not been compromised. 

What you need to do, in case you haven’t acted yet

User and customer communications with instructions on what to do were sent out on November 3. If you haven’t acted yet, these are the actions to complete immediately:

  • All customers using the GitBook API: Create a new API token. We revoked all personal API tokens, but customers’ existing apps need to be updated

  • Customers with connected third-party tools: Rotate any third-party API tokens or secrets you use to connect other tools to GitBook.

  • Customers with integrations: If you have published integrations that use secrets, rotate those secrets.

  • Git Sync (GitHub app): No action needed. We rotated these keys for you.

  • GitLab: No action needed. We rotated these keys for you.

  • Authenticated access with a custom backend: regenerate your authenticated access signing key in the GitBook app and update it in your backend implementation

If you’re unsure what applies to you, contact your account manager or our support team.

Indicators of compromise

We have identified the following IP addresses implicated in this attack:

  • 94.183.188.91

  • 45.139.84.195

  • 198.251.83.217

We recommend you review your environments for any mentions of these IP addresses to ensure that your data hasn’t been compromised.

Impact

Availability

GitBook went offline from 20:32 UTC on 2 Nov to 11:56 UTC on 3 Nov, about 16 hours. Cached published sites stayed up for part of that window.

Scope of the attack

Our investigation indicates the attacker’s activity focused on a single customer, but did have access to the customer data shared above.

Systems accessed

Our internal code repositories, parts of our compute infrastructure, and the deployed code and secrets of our edge network.

Data accessed

Our source code, infrastructure secrets, database credentials, integration tokens and Git Sync secrets.

Data modified

No evidence of any customer content being modified.

Customer action

New API tokens; reconnecting Git Sync and GitLab, if applicable; rotating integration secrets

If anything is found that changes the above picture, we’ll contact affected customers directly.

Timeline (UTC)

11/02/2026 12:27 - First hijacked account at the targeted customer

11/02/2026 16:32 - Attacker gains access to staff sessions, then access to our source code

11/02/2026 17:48 - Attacker reaches our production environment

11/02/2026 18:10 - Internal alert of unauthorized activity; investigation starts

11/02/2026 19:58 - SSO flaw fixed

11/02/2026 20:32 - Compromised accounts disabled; attacker cut off; GitBook app taken offline

11/03/2026 02:34 - Redeployment with new secrets begins; all existing API tokens invalidated

11/03/2026 03:09 - New Cloudflare Workers are deployed

11/03/2026 06:00 - GitBook team begins to prepare a new release with newly cycled credentials

11/03/2026 10:52 - GitHub app keys rotated

11/03/2026 11:56 - All secrets rotated; GitBook fully back online

11/03/2026 22:51 - GitLab tokens used for Git Sync rotated

Next steps

We’ve already closed the paths the attacker used and fixed the exploited vulnerabilities.

We’re making changes to make sure an attack like this can’t happen again. We’re hardening our networking infrastructure, introducing changes to how we manage changes across the stack and investing further in our monitoring and detection capabilities. 

We commit to writing about this incident, our learnings and actions following it, and our broader engineering approach to security practices in the coming weeks and on an ongoing basis. 

We hope that by going into details, we can help other companies avoid the same mistakes that we made.

Why this attack was different & what this means for SaaS security

This wasn’t a broad scan for outdated software. The attacker targeted one of our customers and, once inside, the attacker moved with a speed and precision that pointed to an attack driven largely by automation and AI. 

The sophistication of the attack and how quickly it went from initial incursion to full access would’ve been unthinkable a few years ago.

This is where attacks are heading for every SaaS company. In late 2025, Anthropic reported a campaign in which AI carried out 80–90% of the tactical work. 

For us, three lessons follow:

  1. Every forgotten credential is a liability: Least privilege, short-lived credentials and secret scanning have to be the default.

  2. Response speed has to match attack speed: That means automated detection and a practiced plan to contain fast.

  3. SaaS vendors are a route to their customers: Every SaaS provider is part of its customers’ security perimeter.

We’re applying all three to ourselves first, and we’ll share what we learn.

Our commitment

We’re sorry. We hold ourselves to the highest standards, and we know an incident like this affects the trust you place in GitBook.

We hope the transparency in this post, and the actions we’ve already taken, help rebuild that trust.

If you have questions, contact your account manager or our support team. For live updates, visit status.gitbook.com. 

Sara Tandowsky, GitBook CEO
Samy Pessé, GitBook Co-founder & CTO

translation.html:
2026 年 11 月 4 日，星期三，20:30 CET

事件复盘

概要

2026 年 11 月 2 日，一名攻击者未经授权访问了 GitBook 的系统。

攻击者利用 GitBook 的 SSO 登录流程中的一个漏洞，创建了冒充 GitBook 员工的登录会话。这使其能够查询一个配置错误的 GitHub App 的身份验证信息；该应用作为集成安装在我们的组织中。攻击者由此获得了对我们内部代码仓库的访问权限，并最终获取了一枚 Cloudflare API 密钥。

攻击者利用这枚密钥获取了生产环境中的机密凭据，并通过一个服务账号获得了对基础设施的完整访问权限。

数小时内，我们禁用了所有受影响的内部基础设施服务账号。这阻止了攻击，也导致 GitBook 应用下线。随后，我们轮换了基础设施中的所有机密凭据和 API 密钥，以及由 GitBook 管理的所有客户机密凭据。经过约 16 小时的停机，GitBook 于 11 月 3 日 11:56 UTC 全面恢复上线。

我们目前看到的一切都表明，这次攻击针对的是某一位 GitBook 客户，而非整个 GitBook。我们尚未发现任何其他客户的内容遭到修改的证据。 

在拥有访问权限期间，攻击者能够访问存储在 GitBook 中的客户数据。因此，我们已将所有客户数据视为已暴露，而不仅限于被针对的那位客户。 

我们如何遏制事件并恢复服务

让 GitBook 下线是我们经过慎重考虑后作出的决定。一旦攻击者进入我们的云基础设施，继续运行平台就意味着，在我们处理事件的同时，他们仍可继续寻找访问途径。我们选择承受更长时间的停机，以避免这一风险。

在离线期间，我们轮换了生产基础设施中的所有机密凭据，以及由 GitBook 管理的所有客户机密凭据；使最终截止时间之前签发的所有 API 令牌失效；重新创建了预发布和生产环境中的所有节点；并撤销了被入侵服务账号执行的所有操作。我们还在加强防护措施期间停用了内部管理后台。

这起事件的责任在我们。对于服务中断，以及未能更早与您沟通，我们深表歉意。

下一节将具体说明哪些内容可被访问、我们发现了什么，以及我们采取了哪些措施。

这对您的数据意味着什么

攻击者在 11 月 2 日晚间访问了我们的生产环境，持续约 2 小时 45 分钟，并在 11 月 3 日凌晨再次访问，持续约 40 分钟。 

在此期间，攻击者能够访问以下客户数据：

  • GitBook API 令牌

  • 集成令牌和机密凭据

  • 会话签名密钥 

  • 您的网站访客向 GitBook Assistant 提出的问题

  • 使用身份验证访问的文档网站

  • GitHub 

    • 补充信息：攻击者可以以 GitBook 应用的身份执行操作，但仅限于各客户已授权该应用访问的仓库。我们无法确定攻击者是否在客户仓库中执行过任何操作。我们在下文提供了建议采取的补救措施。

  • GitLab

    • 补充信息：攻击者可以暂时代表 GitBook 在已连接的 GitLab 项目中执行操作，但仅限于各客户已授予访问权限的仓库。我们无法确定攻击者是否在客户仓库中执行过任何操作。我们在下文提供了建议采取的补救措施。

  • 您的内容，例如文档、空间和变更请求

    • 补充信息：我们尚未发现任何其他客户的内容遭到修改的证据

账单信息、密码或 IP 地址未遭泄露。 

如果您尚未采取行动，需要做什么

我们已于 11 月 3 日向用户和客户发送了说明所需操作的通知。如果您尚未采取行动，请立即完成以下操作：

  • 所有使用 GitBook API 的客户：创建新的 API 令牌。我们已撤销所有个人 API 令牌，但客户现有的应用仍需更新

  • 已连接第三方工具的客户： 轮换您用于将其他工具连接至 GitBook 的所有第三方 API 令牌或机密凭据。

  • 使用集成的客户：如果您发布的集成使用了机密凭据，请轮换这些凭据。

  • Git Sync（GitHub 应用）：无需操作。我们已为您轮换这些密钥。

  • GitLab： 无需操作。我们已为您轮换这些密钥。

  • 通过自定义后端实现的身份验证访问：在 GitBook 应用中重新生成身份验证访问签名密钥，并在您的后端实现中更新该密钥

如果您不确定哪些情况适用于您，请联系您的客户经理或我们的支持团队。

入侵指标

我们已确认以下 IP 地址涉及此次攻击：

  • 94.183.188.91

  • 45.139.84.195

  • 198.251.83.217

我们建议您检查自身环境中是否出现过这些 IP 地址，以确保您的数据未遭泄露或篡改。

影响

可用性

GitBook 从 11 月 2 日 20:32 UTC 至 11 月 3 日 11:56 UTC 处于离线状态，持续约 16 小时。在此期间的一部分时间内，已缓存的发布网站仍可访问。

攻击范围

我们的调查表明，攻击者的活动集中于单一客户，但其确实能够访问上述客户数据。

被访问的系统

我们的内部代码仓库、部分计算基础设施，以及边缘网络中部署的代码和机密凭据。

被访问的数据

我们的源代码、基础设施机密凭据、数据库凭据、集成令牌和 Git Sync 机密凭据。

被修改的数据

没有证据表明任何客户内容遭到修改。

客户需采取的行动

创建新的 API 令牌；重新连接 Git Sync 和 GitLab（如适用）；轮换集成机密凭据

如果发现任何改变上述情况的信息，我们会直接联系受影响的客户。

时间线（UTC）

11/02/2026 12:27 - 目标客户的首个账号遭到劫持

11/02/2026 16:32 - 攻击者获得员工会话的访问权限，随后获得对我们源代码的访问权限

11/02/2026 17:48 - 攻击者进入我们的生产环境

11/02/2026 18:10 - 内部发出未经授权活动的警报；调查开始

11/02/2026 19:58 - SSO 漏洞修复

11/02/2026 20:32 - 被入侵的账号被禁用；攻击者的访问被切断；GitBook 应用下线

11/03/2026 02:34 - 开始使用新的机密凭据重新部署；所有现有 API 令牌失效

11/03/2026 03:09 - 新的 Cloudflare Workers 部署完成

11/03/2026 06:00 - GitBook 团队开始准备使用新轮换凭据的新版本

11/03/2026 10:52 - GitHub 应用密钥轮换完成

11/03/2026 11:56 - 所有机密凭据轮换完成；GitBook 全面恢复上线

11/03/2026 22:51 - 用于 Git Sync 的 GitLab 令牌轮换完成

后续措施

我们已经封堵攻击者使用的路径，并修复了被利用的漏洞。

我们正在作出调整，以确保此类攻击不再发生。我们正在加固网络基础设施，改进整个技术栈的变更管理方式，并进一步投入资源提升监控和检测能力。 

我们承诺，在未来几周及此后持续撰文，介绍此次事件、从中吸取的教训及后续行动，以及我们在安全实践方面更广泛的工程方法。 

我们希望，通过详细披露，能够帮助其他公司避免重蹈我们的覆辙。

这次攻击有何不同，以及它对 SaaS 安全意味着什么

这并非针对过时软件的广泛扫描。攻击者针对的是我们的一位客户，而在进入系统后，其行动速度和精确程度表明，这次攻击主要由自动化和 AI 驱动。 

攻击的复杂程度，以及从最初入侵到获得完整访问权限的速度，在几年前是难以想象的。

这是每一家 SaaS 公司都将面临的攻击趋势。2025 年末，Anthropic 报告了一场攻击行动，其中 AI 完成了 80–90% 的战术工作。 

对我们而言，由此可以得出三条教训：

  1. 每一项被遗忘的凭据都是隐患：最小权限、短期凭据和机密凭据扫描必须成为默认做法。

  2. 响应速度必须跟上攻击速度：这意味着需要自动化检测，以及经过演练、能够迅速遏制攻击的预案。

  3. SaaS 供应商是通向其客户的路径：每一家 SaaS 提供商都是其客户安全边界的一部分。

我们会首先将这三条落实到自身，并分享从中学到的经验。

我们的承诺

我们深表歉意。我们以最高标准要求自己，也明白此类事件会影响您对 GitBook 的信任。

我们希望，本文的透明披露，以及我们已经采取的行动，能够帮助重建这份信任。

如果您有任何问题，请联系您的客户经理或我们的支持团队。如需查看实时更新，请访问 status.gitbook.com。 

Sara Tandowsky，GitBook 首席执行官
Samy Pessé，GitBook 联合创始人兼首席技术官
